blocks.text: Nobody wants to hand write JSON-RPC messages every time they build an MCP server.
The official TypeScript SDK gives you classes and helper methods instead, so registering a tool takes a few lines, not a hand rolled parser.
This lesson covers the McpServer and Client classes, the three registration helpers, and connecting a server over stdio or HTTP.
1. What the TypeScript SDK Is
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450715-754643952.png
It is the official library, published as modelcontextprotocol slash sdk, for building MCP servers and clients in TypeScript or plain JavaScript.
It wraps the raw JSON-RPC message format from the spec inside ordinary classes, so you write handlers instead of message parsers.
The same package exports both server side and client side pieces, so one project can hold a server, a client, or both.

items: Capability negotiation during the initialize handshake
Converting Zod schemas into JSON Schema for the wire
Ready made stdio and HTTP transport implementations
Consistent error shapes across every tool, resource, and prompt call

blocks.text: Because the SDK is maintained alongside the specification, it tends to pick up new protocol features soon after they are finalized.
2. Installing the SDK and Setting Up a Project
A typical project starts as an ordinary Node and TypeScript setup, with the SDK and Zod added as dependencies.

code.content:
npm init -y
npm install @modelcontextprotocol/sdk zod
npm install -D typescript tsx

# project layout
my-server/
  src/index.ts
  package.json
  tsconfig.json

blocks.text: Zod is worth calling out specifically, it is the schema library the SDK uses to describe and validate tool input at runtime.
3. The McpServer Class and Its Constructor Options

blocks.alt: The McpServer Class and Its Constructor Options
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450715-276744765.png
Every server starts by constructing an McpServer instance, passing a name and a version string that identify it to any client that connects.
An optional capabilities field lets you hint which features the server plans to expose, though registering tools and resources normally covers this automatically.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Constructor option","Type","Purpose"],"rows":[["name","string","Identifies the server to a connecting client"],["version","string","Reported during the initialize handshake"],["capabilities","object, optional","Advertises optional features up front"]]}

blocks.title: A server is not listening until connected
blocks.content: Creating an McpServer only builds the object in memory. It cannot receive a single message until you connect it to a transport.

blocks.text: 4. The Client Class and Its Constructor Options
The same package exports a Client class, useful for building a custom host, an automated test, or a script that talks to a server directly.
Its constructor takes the same shape as McpServer, a name and a version, since both sides identify themselves the same way during the handshake.
5. Registering a Tool with server.tool
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450716-176060995.png
Tools are registered by calling server.tool with a name, a short description, a Zod schema for the input, and a handler function.
The handler receives already validated, typed arguments, and returns a small object with a content array rather than a bare value.
6. Zod Schemas for Tool Input Validation

blocks.alt: Zod Schemas for Tool Input Validation
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450946-767166935.png
The SDK converts a Zod schema into the JSON Schema a client sees over the wire, and validates every incoming call against it before your handler runs.

blocks.title: Write descriptions a model can act on
blocks.content: A schema field named priority is less useful than one described as controls how urgently this is handled, with an enum of allowed values.

blocks.text: 7. Registering a Resource with server.resource
Resources are registered with a name, a URI, and a handler that returns the resource content wrapped in a contents array.
A resource handler should stay read only. Its job is to describe what the data looks like right now, not to change any state.
8. Resource Templates for Dynamic URIs
A ResourceTemplate helper describes a URI pattern with curly brace placeholders, which the SDK extracts and passes to your handler as parameters.
9. Registering a Prompt with server.prompt
Prompts follow the same pattern once more, a name, a Zod schema for any parameters, and a handler returning a list of messages.
A registered prompt shows up in a host application as a pickable template, so a user can trigger it without typing anything by hand.
10. Connecting a Server to a Stdio Transport

blocks.alt: Connecting a Server to a Stdio Transport
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450947-596756869.png
A stdio transport is the simplest option, meant for a server a host spawns as a local subprocess and talks to over standard input and output.
Connecting a transport is the moment a server actually starts listening. Before that call it is just an object sitting in memory.
11. Connecting a Server to an HTTP Transport
For a server that runs independently and needs to serve many clients over the network, the SDK ships a streamable HTTP transport instead.
The sessionIdGenerator option controls whether the server tracks a session per client, useful once more than one client can connect at a time.
12. Using the Client Class to Connect and Call Tools
A client connects to a matching transport, then can list and call whatever the server has registered.
This same client class is what you would reach for to write an automated test against your own server, no host application required.
13. The Shape of Returned Content
Every tool handler returns an object with a content array, letting a single result carry plain text, an image, or other content types together.
Returning a bare string instead of this wrapped shape is one of the most common early mistakes when moving from a plain function to an SDK handler.
14. Handling Errors with McpError
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450948-553181626.png
A plain thrown Error is caught by the SDK and reported back as a tool error, but McpError lets you attach a specific protocol level error code.
A specific error code helps a model tell the difference between a bad request it can fix and a failure it cannot do anything about.
15. Why Use the Official SDK Instead of Hand Rolling JSON-RPC

blocks.alt: Why Use the Official SDK Instead of Hand Rolling JSON-RPC
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450948-774483779.png
Writing raw JSON-RPC means manually building request and response objects, tracking ids, and handling every edge case the spec defines.

items: Correct message framing and id tracking come for free
Capability negotiation during initialize is handled automatically
Zod schemas give you both runtime validation and JSON Schema generation
Transport implementations are tested against the real specification
Upgrades to a new protocol revision usually mean upgrading one package

blocks.title: Hand rolled servers tend to drift from the spec
blocks.content: A small mistake in message framing can work fine against one client and fail silently against another. The SDK closes that gap for you.

Common Mistakes

items: Skipping Zod validation and accepting a loosely typed object, losing runtime safety and schema quality together
Returning a bare string instead of a wrapped content array from a tool handler
Forgetting to call server.connect, so the server never actually starts listening
Giving a resource handler side effects, when it should stay a pure read
Throwing a plain string instead of an Error or McpError, losing useful error detail
Choosing HTTP for a purely local single client server when stdio would be simpler

blocks.text: Practice
Build a small server with one tool that converts a temperature between celsius and fahrenheit, using an enum for the target unit.

items: Stretch goal, add a resource that lists every conversion the tool has performed so far
Stretch goal, connect a Client to your server and call the tool from a short test script

blocks.text: Key Takeaway
The TypeScript SDK turns MCP servers into ordinary classes and method calls, McpServer and Client on the outside, Zod schemas describing the inside.
Reaching for the official SDK instead of hand rolled JSON-RPC buys correctness, spec compliance, and an upgrade path, for the cost of one dependency.
